newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's Perez to burst back into limelight.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's Perez to burst back into limelight.

text.p: Venezuela's former President Carlos Andres Perez completes more than two years under house arrest on Wednesday with all the pent-up energy of a champagne cork.
Drummed out of office in May 1993 to face corruption charges just eight months short of completing his second presidential term, the flamboyant Perez plans a quick return to public life.
"You will see Carlos Andres Perez elected senator for Tachira state," he said late on Monday in an interview in the luxurious home above the capital that has been his jail for the past 28 months.
Perez, 73, still maintains that he was wrongly convicted for misappropriating $17 million in state funds.

"My conscience is quite clear because I know that although I have made many mistakes there is nothing in my public life which can shame me and this makes me impervious to all these slanders they have poured onto me," he said defiantly.
Perez expects a festive atmosphere to accompany his release at midnight on Wednesday, which should stir up the Venezuelan political scene.
Perez said he was receiving an average of 100 visitors a day in recent weeks. "I don't think ... my reputation has been damaged," he said.

His path to political redemption will start with a tour of western Venezuela, beginning with his home state of Tachira on the Colombian border, where the former leader still commands considerable support.

Although expelled by the social democratic party, Democratic Action (AD), he helped to found 55 years ago, Perez has spoken at various times in recent weeks of "recovering" the party he twice led to election wins and of setting up a new political movement.
Elected for a second term by a landslide majority in 1988, Perez's government was shaken by bloody riots in 1989 and two coup attempts in 1992 as it attempted to push through tough economic reforms.
After a brief stay at the low-security El Junquito prison in Caracas, Perez opted to exercise his right, due to his age, to serve his term under house arrest.
Even at home Perez maintained a high public profile through regular press interviews and more recently chats on the Internet.
